hypotheses.title: ChainlinkOracle lacks staleness and round-completeness checks
hypotheses.description: `_getLatestPrice` reads `latestRoundData()` but discards `roundID`, `startedAt`, and `answeredInRound`, and never compares `timeStamp` against `block.timestamp`. Only `price > 0` is enforced. If the feed is stale (e.g., market halted, L2 sequencer down, or feed deprecated), the oracle keeps returning the last price indefinitely, and the Operator uses it for collateral valuation and liquidation math.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits for a Chainlink feed to go stale (or for the L2 sequencer to be down) while the underlying asset price moves sharply. 2) Attacker borrows against the stale-priced collateral at the inflated old price, or liquidates a healthy borrower using the stale price. 3) Because `_getLatestPrice` never reverts on staleness, the borrow/liquidation succeeds at the wrong price.
hypotheses.impact: Under-collateralized borrows drain the market; incorrect liquidations seize collateral from healthy users; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `block.timestamp - timeStamp <= stalenessThreshold`, require `answeredInRound >= roundID`, and add an L2 sequencer uptime feed check.

hypotheses.title: MixedPriceOracleV4 uses stale eOracle price when api3 is fresh but delta is high
hypotheses.description: When `apiV3Fresh` is true but `deltaBps > deltaSymbol`, the code falls back to the eOracle price and only checks `block.timestamp - eOracleUpdatedAt < _staleness`. However, if `eOraclePrice <= 0` the `uint256(eOraclePrice)` cast silently wraps to a huge number, and the delta computation `_absDiff` on a negative eOracle price produces a nonsensical ratio. More importantly, the fallback branch does not verify `eOraclePrice > 0` before casting, so a zero/negative eOracle price is accepted as a valid price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that the eOracle feed returns 0 or a negative value (feed failure). 2) Attacker triggers a borrow/liquidation that routes through the fallback branch (api3 fresh but delta high, or api3 stale). 3) `uint256(eOraclePrice)` wraps to `2**256 - x`, producing an astronomically large price used for collateral valuation.
hypotheses.impact: Massive mispricing of collateral/debt; attacker can borrow far more than collateral is worth or liquidate healthy positions; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `eOraclePrice > 0` (and `apiV3Price > 0`) before casting to `uint256`, and revert on non-positive prices.

hypotheses.title: Referral signature lacks chainId and contract address, replayable cross-chain
hypotheses.description: The signed message hash is `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, referrer, nonces[msg.sender]))` with no chainId and no address(this). The nonce is per-user and only incremented on the same contract, so an identical signature is valid on any other deployment of ReferralSigning (or any fork) where the same user has the same nonce. An attacker who observes a valid referral signature on one chain can replay it on another chain to register the referral there.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim signs referral message for referrer R on chain A. 2) Attacker observes signature (mempool / logs / off-chain). 3) Attacker submits the same signature on chain B's ReferralSigning deployment where victim's nonce is still 0. 4) Signature recovers to victim, referral is claimed on chain B without victim's consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized referral registration on other chains; referral rewards/attribution misallocated; user's referral slot permanently consumed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` and `address(this)` in the signed payload, and use EIP-712 typed structured data.

hypotheses.title: mTokenGateway.outHere sends funds to journal sender, not receiver
hypotheses.description: `_outHere` overwrites the caller-supplied `receiver` with `_sender` decoded from the journal ("temporary overwrite"), then transfers underlying to `_sender`. The `receiver` parameter is only used in the event. Any user who supplies a valid journal (or a proof-forwarder who batches) will have funds delivered to the journal's `_sender`, not the intended receiver, and the event misleads off-chain accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls `outHere` with a journal whose `_sender` is an attacker-controlled address and a `receiver` they claim is a victim; the contract transfers underlying to `_sender` (attacker) while emitting an event showing `receiver`. Alternatively, a legitimate receiver never gets funds because the code ignores the parameter.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds / wrong recipient accounting; users expecting funds at `receiver` receive nothing while `_sender` gets them.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `receiver = _sender` overwrite and transfer to the caller-supplied `receiver` (or revert if the parameter is intentionally unused).

hypotheses.title: mErc20Host external ops overwrite receiver with journal sender
hypotheses.description: All three internal handlers unconditionally set `receiver = _sender` from the decoded journal, discarding the caller-supplied `receiver`. Minted mTokens, repaid credit, and liquidated collateral are therefore attributed to the journal's `_sender` regardless of what the caller requested, and the emitted events report the wrong receiver.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted caller (or a proof-forwarder) submits a journal whose `_sender` is attacker-controlled while passing a different `receiver`; the protocol credits the attacker's address with mTokens/repayment/liquidation proceeds, and the event logs a misleading receiver.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds / misattributed balances; users cannot direct mint/repay/liquidate proceeds to the intended address.
hypotheses.recommendation: Delete the `receiver = _sender` overwrite and use the caller-supplied `receiver` consistently in state updates and events.

hypotheses.title: mTokenGateway outHere allows forwarder to redirect funds to arbitrary sender
hypotheses.description: `_checkSender` permits `msg.sender == owner()` or any PROOF_FORWARDER / PROOF_BATCH_FORWARDER to bypass the `msgSender == srcSender` check. The journal's `_sender` is then used as the recipient of `IERC20(underlying).safeTransfer(_sender, amount)`. A forwarder can therefore submit a journal with `_sender = attacker` and drain the gateway's underlying balance up to `_accAmountOut - accAmountOut[_sender]`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds PROOF_FORWARDER role. 2) Attacker crafts journal with `_sender = attacker`, `_market = gateway`, `_chainId = LINEA_CHAIN_ID`, `_dstChainId = block.chainid`, `_accAmountOut` large. 3) Calls `outHere` with `amount` up to the difference. 4) `_checkSender` passes; `safeTransfer(_sender, amount)` sends underlying to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of bridged underlying tokens held by the gateway; loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == _sender` for the transfer recipient, or bind the journal to the caller via signature/proof that includes msg.sender.

hypotheses.title: Pauser can pause Redeem/Repay/Transfer, permanently trapping user funds
hypotheses.description: `_pauseAllMarketOperations` pauses `Redeem`, `Repay`, `Transfer`, and `Liquidate` in addition to supply/borrow operations. Once paused, `beforeMTokenRedeem` and `beforeMTokenRepay` revert, so users cannot withdraw their supplied underlying nor repay debt. Only the owner can unpause (`setPaused` requires `msg.sender == owner()` for unpause). If the owner key is lost or the owner is malicious/compromised, all user funds are permanently locked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) PAUSE_MANAGER role (or owner) calls `emergencyPauseMarket(market)`. 2) All operations including Redeem/Repay/Transfer are paused. 3) Users cannot withdraw or repay. 4) Only owner can unpause; if owner is unavailable, funds are stuck forever.
hypotheses.impact: Complete freeze of user funds in the market; users cannot redeem collateral or repay debt, leading to forced liquidations once unpaused or permanent loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Never pause Redeem/Repay/Transfer, or add a timelock/guardian-based unpause path so users can always exit.

hypotheses.title: mTokenGateway outHere allows replay of same journal to drain underlying
hypotheses.description: `outHere` verifies the proof and then checks `_accAmountOut - accAmountOut[_sender] >= amount`, incrementing `accAmountOut[_sender]` by `amount`. The journal contains `_accAmountOut` which is the cumulative amount out from the host. If the same journal is submitted multiple times with different `amount` values that are each less than the remaining allowance, the check passes each time and `accAmountOut` is incremented, but the underlying is transferred out each time. There is no nonce or per-journal replay protection, and the `_checkSender` only checks that the caller is allowed, not that the journal has not been used. An attacker who can obtain a valid journal (e.g., by observing a legitimate proof) can replay it with smaller amounts to drain the gateway's underlying balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a valid `journalData` and `seal` for a legitimate `outHere` call with a large `_accAmountOut`. 2) Attacker calls `outHere` with the same journal but `amount = 1` repeatedly. 3) Each call passes `_accAmountOut - accAmountOut[_sender] >= 1` and transfers 1 wei to the attacker. 4) Attacker repeats until `accAmountOut[_sender]` reaches `_accAmountOut`, draining the gateway's balance up to the journal's allowance.
hypotheses.impact: Gateway underlying drained; legitimate users cannot withdraw; protocol insolvent on the extension chain.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a per-journal nonce or hash-based replay protection, and ensure each journal can only be consumed once.

hypotheses.title: Operator.initialize can be front-run by anyone
hypotheses.description: `Operator.initialize` is `public initializer` with no access restriction. Although `_disableInitializers()` is called in the constructor, if the contract is deployed behind a proxy (as the `OwnableUpgradeable` and `initializer` pattern implies), the implementation's constructor runs once, but the proxy's storage is uninitialized. An attacker can call `initialize` on the proxy first, setting themselves as `_admin` (owner) and controlling `rolesOperator`, `blacklistOperator`, and `rewardDistributor`. This grants full owner privileges to the attacker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Protocol deploys `Operator` behind a proxy. 2. Before the legitimate deployer calls `initialize`, attacker calls `initialize(attacker, attacker, attacker, attacker)`. 3. Attacker becomes owner and can call all `onlyOwner` functions (setPriceOracle, supportMarket, setCollateralFactor, etc.).
hypotheses.impact: Complete protocol takeover: attacker controls oracle, markets, collateral factors, reward distributor, and can drain funds via malicious oracle prices.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `onlyOwner` or deployer-only guard to `initialize`, or use a factory that atomically deploys and initializes.

hypotheses.title: ChainlinkOracle.getUnderlyingPrice uses symbol lookup, vulnerable to symbol collision
hypotheses.description: The oracle keys feeds by `symbol` string (`priceFeeds[symbol]`), and `getUnderlyingPrice` derives the symbol from `ImTokenMinimal(mToken).underlying()).symbol()`. Any ERC20 whose `symbol()` returns a string matching a registered feed (e.g., a fake "USDC" token) will be priced using the real feed. Since `supportMarket` only checks `isListed` and the oracle is consulted at borrow/liquidation time, an attacker can deploy a token with a colliding symbol and get it listed (if the owner lists it) or, more directly, use it as collateral in a market whose symbol collides.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a worthless ERC20 whose `symbol()` returns "USDC" (or any registered symbol). 2) If the market is listed (or via any path that calls `getUnderlyingPrice` on that token), the oracle returns the real USDC price. 3) Attacker mints the fake token, supplies it as collateral, and borrows real assets against it.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker borrows real assets against worthless collateral; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Key feeds by token address (or by a unique market identifier) instead of by symbol string.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in mTokenGateway.outHere via ERC20 transfer callback
hypotheses.description: In `_outHere`, the contract updates `accAmountOut[_sender] += amount` (effects) and then performs `IERC20(underlying).safeTransfer(_sender, amount)` (interactions). If the underlying token is an ERC-777 or otherwise has transfer hooks (or the receiver is a contract that reenters), the receiver can reenter `outHere` before the outer call completes. Because the accounting update happens before the transfer, the reentrant call sees the updated `accAmountOut` and can drain additional funds up to the journal's `_accAmountOut` limit. The `nonReentrant` guard is absent on `outHere` and `_outHere`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid journal with a large `_accAmountOut` for their address. 2) Calls `outHere` with an amount. 3) During `safeTransfer`, the underlying token's hook (or a malicious receiver contract) reenters `outHere` with another amount. 4) The reentrant call passes the `_accAmountOut - accAmountOut[_sender] >= amount` check because the outer call already incremented `accAmountOut`. 5) Repeat to drain the gateway's underlying balance.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of all underlying tokens held by the gateway; other users' funds drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `outHere` and/or move the `accAmountOut` update after the transfer, or use a checks-effects-interactions pattern with a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: Blacklisted user can be liquidated but cannot repay, trapping their position
hypotheses.description: `beforeMTokenRepay` enforces `onlyAllowedUser(borrower)` and `ifNotBlacklisted` is applied to the borrower in `beforeMTokenLiquidate`/`beforeMTokenSeize`, but `beforeMTokenRepay` only checks `onlyAllowedUser(borrower)` (whitelist) and does NOT check blacklist. However, `beforeMTokenLiquidate` requires `ifNotBlacklisted(borrower)`, so a blacklisted borrower cannot be liquidated. Meanwhile `beforeMTokenRepay` requires `onlyAllowedUser(borrower)` — if whitelist is enabled and the borrower is not whitelisted, no one (not even a third party) can repay on their behalf. The borrower's debt keeps accruing interest with no path to repay or liquidate.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin blacklists a borrower (or enables whitelist and removes borrower). 2) Borrower's position becomes unhealthy. 3) Liquidators call `liquidate` → `beforeMTokenLiquidate` reverts on `ifNotBlacklisted(borrower)`. 4) Third parties call `repayBehalf` → `beforeMTokenRepay` reverts on `onlyAllowedUser(borrower)`. 5) Position is permanently stuck, debt grows unbounded.
hypotheses.impact: Borrower's collateral is permanently frozen; protocol accrues bad debt that can never be cleared; lenders cannot recover funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow repay/liquidation of blacklisted or non-whitelisted borrowers (repay should not be gated on borrower's whitelist/blacklist status), or provide an admin rescue path.

hypotheses.title: mErc20Host external ops accept journals without binding to msg.sender
hypotheses.description: `_checkSender` allows `msg.sender == admin` or any address holding PROOF_FORWARDER / PROOF_BATCH_FORWARDER role to bypass the `msgSender == srcSender` check. Combined with `_checkProofCall` only verifying `dstChainId == block.chainid`, `market == address(this)` and `allowedChains[chainId]`, a proof-forwarder (or admin) can submit a journal whose `_sender` is an arbitrary victim, causing `_mintExternal`/`_repayExternal`/`_liquidateExternal` to credit/debit the victim's account. The journal itself is not bound to the caller, so any proof-forwarder can redirect operations to any user.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains PROOF_FORWARDER role (or is admin). 2) Attacker crafts a journal with `_sender = victim`, `_market = this`, valid `_chainId`/`_dstChainId`. 3) Calls `mintExternal`/`repayExternal`/`liquidateExternal` with the journal. 4) `_checkSender` passes because msg.sender is a forwarder; `acc[_chainId].inPerChain[victim]` is incremented and victim's mToken balance is minted/repaid.
hypotheses.impact: Forced mint/repay/liquidation on arbitrary users; accounting corruption of `acc.inPerChain`; potential theft via forced liquidation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the journal's `_sender` to `msg.sender` (or to the recovered signer of the proof) and remove the admin/forwarder bypass for the sender check.

hypotheses.title: mTokenGateway.supplyOnHost credits receiver without whitelist check
hypotheses.description: `supplyOnHost` applies `onlyAllowedUser(msg.sender)` and `ifNotBlacklisted(msg.sender)`/`ifNotBlacklisted(receiver)`, but does not apply `onlyAllowedUser(receiver)`. When whitelist is enabled, an attacker can supply on behalf of a non-whitelisted receiver, incrementing `accAmountIn[receiver]` and enabling that receiver to later withdraw via `outHere` (which also lacks a whitelist check on the receiver). This bypasses the whitelist gate for the receiving side.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (whitelisted) calls `supplyOnHost(amount, victimOrAttackerControlledReceiver, selector)`; `accAmountIn[receiver]` is credited. The receiver then calls `outHere` (no whitelist check) to extract underlying, effectively laundering whitelist status.
hypotheses.impact: Whitelist bypass; unauthorized users can obtain and withdraw protocol funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyAllowedUser(receiver)` to `supplyOnHost` and to `outHere` (or enforce whitelist on the credited account in both directions).

hypotheses.title: Reward index not updated on transfer, allowing double-claim of MALDA rewards
hypotheses.description: `beforeMTokenTransfer` updates the supply index and distributes rewards for both `src` and `dst`, but the mToken `_transferTokens` moves `accountTokens` without any reward-distributor hook on the destination side after the balance change. Because `_distributeSupplierMalda` is called before the token balance is actually updated, the `dst` accrues rewards based on its pre-transfer balance, and the `src` accrues on its pre-transfer balance too. A user can therefore move tokens between two accounts they control (or to a fresh account) and have both accounts accrue rewards on the same tokens for the same period, then claim from both.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds mTokens in account A. 2) Attacker calls `transfer(B, amount)` where B is a second account they control. 3) `beforeMTokenTransfer` distributes rewards to A (on full balance) and to B (on B's old balance). 4) After transfer, B holds the tokens but its supplier index was already synced to the current index, so B will accrue rewards on the new balance from the next index update onward, while A already captured rewards on the same tokens up to the transfer. 5) Attacker repeats transfers back and forth across many accounts to multiply accrued rewards, then calls `claimMalda` on each account.
hypotheses.impact: Inflation of MALDA reward claims far beyond the intended emission schedule; reward pool drained; honest suppliers receive diluted rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Distribute rewards for `src` and `dst` after the balance change, or sync the destination's supplier index to the current index before crediting the new balance so no double accrual occurs.
